title: After the Rochester Tornado, a Sister Asked a Doctor for a Hospital
dek: After the tornado of August 1883, Mother Alfred Moes proposed a hospital to Dr W. W. Mayo; he said Rochester was too small, and her sisters spent six years making it happen.

story.founder: Mother Alfred Moes and the Sisters of St Francis, with William Worrall Mayo
story.company: Saint Marys Hospital, Rochester (later Mayo Clinic Hospital, Saint Marys Campus)
story.event: Proposing, funding and opening a hospital after the 1883 Rochester tornado
story.summary: After a tornado struck Rochester, Minnesota, on 21 August 1883, Dr William Worrall Mayo ran a makeshift hospital nursed under the supervision of the Sisters of St Francis. Their superior, Mother Alfred Moes, then proposed a permanent hospital; Mayo thought the town too small, but agreed to take charge if the sisters paid for it. The sisters saved for about four years, bought land in 1887 and opened Saint Marys Hospital on 30 September 1889 with the Mayos as its physicians.
paragraphs: On the evening of 21 August 1883 a tornado tore through the north of Rochester, Minnesota. A desk clock carried a block by the wind was found stopped at twenty-four minutes to seven. Scarcely a house in Lower Town was left standing. By lantern light, rescuers carried the injured to hotels and offices; some forty were laid on the parlour floors of the convent of the Sisters of St Francis. The storm killed 37 people along its path, by the National Weather Service's count.

Dr William Worrall Mayo was put in charge of a temporary hospital in Rommel's dance hall. Needing nurses who could give their whole time, he went to the convent one morning and told its superior, Mother Alfred Moes, "There ought to be a sister down there to look after those fellows." She sent two sisters at once, and sisters supervised the nursing until the makeshift hospital closed.

Some time later Mother Alfred called on Mayo with a larger idea: a permanent hospital, where there was none nearby. Her sisters were trained to teach, not nurse. Mayo said no. The town was too small, he told her, a hospital would cost a great deal and it was unlikely to succeed; many people then thought of hospitals as places to die. She replied that if he would take charge, the sisters would pay for it. When he warned it might cost 40,000 dollars, she said they would spend that and more. They agreed with a handshake, and no written contract.

For nearly four years the sisters saved. They gave music lessons, crocheted and embroidered linens to sell, wore two-dollar shoes and ate plain food. In 1887 the congregation voted to build and paid 2,200 dollars in cash for nine acres west of town; Mayo and his son Will toured eastern hospitals to plan the building. Saint Marys Hospital opened on 30 September 1889 with an operation: Dr Charles Mayo removed a cancer of the eye, Will assisted and their father gave the anaesthetic. It was open to all, Mother Alfred said, because "the cause of suffering humanity knows no religion and no sex." In 1904 Mayo wrote a public letter in the newspaper so that the sisters would be credited with the idea and the money.

quote.text: Riches are for spending, and spending for honor and good actions. Therefore extraordinary expense must be limited by the worth of the occasion; for voluntary undoing, may be as well for a man's country, as for the kingdom of heaven.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon allows great expense when the occasion is worth it, and even a voluntary undoing for a higher cause. The sisters lived on plain food and two-dollar shoes for four years to build a hospital Mayo thought too risky. By Bacon's measure, the worth of the occasion was what settled it.

reflection: Mayo's no was a reasonable one, and he gave his reasons plainly. What follows is just as worth noticing. Once the sisters had the money, he chose the site, studied other hospitals and took charge, and years later he went out of his way to make sure the credit went to them.

You will doubt some of your colleagues' ideas, and sometimes you will be right to. It is possible to say so honestly and still help fully once the decision is made. And when something goes well, it is worth asking whose push really started it, and saying so out loud.
invitation: Think of one thing in your work or home that is going well because someone else pushed for it early. Tell that person today, in a sentence or two, what they started.

research_notes: Credit: Clapesattle (1941), the standard history, says the Mayos were often wrongly credited with the idea and records Dr W. W. Mayo's 1894 address and 1904 newspaper letter crediting the Sisters of St Francis with 'the inception' and 'the funds'; the story credits Mother Alfred and the sisters with proposing and paying for the hospital and Mayo with taking medical charge. Clapesattle also notes that Bishop John Ireland had suggested a hospital to Mother Alfred shortly before the tornado and that she did not then favour it; the story leaves this out for length but does not claim the idea was wholly new. Deaths: the National Weather Service gives 37 killed and 200 injured for the tornado that crossed Rochester (its whole path, including Dodge County); Clapesattle records about a score buried in one day in Rochester and three or four later deaths; St. Anthony Messenger says 'dozens'. The story gives the NWS figure and says it covers the storm's path. Cost: Mayo's warning of $40,000 is in Clapesattle and KAAL (KAAL's modern-dollar conversion is clearly wrong and is not used); St. Anthony Messenger's remark that the hospital came in $20,000 under projected cost is unexplained and not used. Beds: modern accounts (St. Anthony Messenger) say 27 beds, while 1889 newspaper descriptions quoted by Clapesattle give a capacity of 45, and Sister Joseph noted the papers described some features only hoped for; the story gives no bed count. Mother Alfred's age at the time differs (born 1828 per Mayo's history site, 1829 per Clapesattle), so no age is given. Mayo's exact 1883 words to her are known only through his own recollection in 1894, so they are paraphrased. The opening operation on 30 September 1889, a day before the planned start, is from Clapesattle. Clapesattle is cited from the Internet Archive's scanned text (Digital Library of India copy). The Bacon passage is the opening of 'Of Expense' (essay 28 in the 1625 order).
